A voice agent talks and acts in the same conversation. So how do you test one properly? This is how the Voice Harness works, what it measured, and where the evidence stops.

Text-only testing misses what matters. A speech-to-speech service speaks and calls tools in one stream, and audio can reach a customer before anyone reads a transcript. Services also differ in interruption, truncation, tool handling and usage reporting. So capabilities need evidence, not vendor claims.

The harness wraps the service under test. A scenario runner synthesises the caller and streams it in twenty millisecond chunks. A provider adapter translates each vendor's transport into one closed set of events, and records a hash of each native payload. An orchestrator then routes everything down two controlled paths.

The first is the action path. Tool proposals pass a guardrail, then a gateway, before reaching a synthetic bank. Protected calls are denied before execution unless identity and confirmation state allow them. Confirmations and approval tokens are single use and consumed transactionally, and bank state is isolated per run.

The second is the audio path. Provider audio is held in immutable units that carry a hash, a sample range and epochs. Independent speech recognition and assessment inform a policy decision. Only approved audio is released, through a single-use token bound to the client session, and each release is recorded. A stale or mismatched approval cannot authorise one.

Everything lands in an append-only, hash-chained ledger. Exports carry a canonical manifest and a digital signature, and verify offline against a trusted key. Evidence-write failure blocks tool calls and audio release. And missing evidence is untestable. It is never treated as a pass.

Here is exactly who decides what. Deterministic rules, plus independent speech recognition, decide every scored criterion: identity, spoken facts, confirmations, audio, and the tools proposed. Model behaviour and platform protection are separate verdicts. One criterion, customer care, is judged by AI, and it sits outside the verdict and the quality score. Two judges reviewed every bake-off run, an OpenAI model and Claude on Bedrock. They changed no scored number, and no calibration has been approved.

Fairness was tested as hard as the vendors. A bias review found the harness counted one point two seconds of trailing silence as latency for three explicit-commit services, which had put Nova first. Corrected, the ranking changed, and quality turned out to be tied. We fixed the timing anchor, gave explicit commits a common five hundred millisecond delay, and took latency out of the ranking, because turn control still differs by service.

The process is rule-based. Prompts are standardised and frozen once scoring starts. A cell is rerun only when a ledger rule shows the sample was lost to a fault outside the model, applied to every provider alike, and an answer a service simply got wrong is never rerun. Ten cells were rerun that way, after rate limits and an adapter fault. The reruns moved scores, so each one is listed in the run notes. Known asymmetries stay disclosed: voices, how Nova receives confirmations, ElevenLabs' backing model, and GPT-Live's earlier-prompt results.

The results. No prohibited actions in six hundred runs. Completion ranged from twenty-nine to thirty-six of thirty-six. Every decided spoken-fact check passed. And median voice cost differed about eightfold. Quality is the part to read carefully.

Quality scored between ninety-seven point six and ninety-nine point six percent, with intervals that overlap, resampled over scenarios. After Holm correction, no pair of services is separable. With forty scenarios, three repetitions and a hundred and twenty paired runs per pair, confirming a two point gap would need roughly three to five hundred runs. So we report a tie, not a ranking.

Latency was measured separately, with every service on its own end-of-speech detection: four hundred and ninety-seven timed turns. Median first audio was one point two to two point one seconds for plain answers, and one point four to two point two with a tool call. For the four services that report it, nine tenths to one point two seconds is just waiting to be sure the caller finished. So there is no speed ranking.

The limits are real. Callers are one scripted synthetic voice, with no accents or interruptions in the main results. Samples are small, as shown. Fact and safe-speech checks depend on one transcriber, from the same vendor as one tested service. Judge identities are masked, but reply style can still give a service away, and the judges are not calibrated. Live runs are host-run, not containerised. And nothing here baselines Amazon Connect or our internal platforms.

What comes next is technical. Put Amazon Connect and our internal agentic platforms behind the same adapter contract, and baseline them against these prototypes on the same scenarios. Calibrate the judges against real transcripts, and complete the human validation. Broaden callers to accents, noise and telephone lines. And gate regressions in C I, since the deterministic core needs no credentials.
